one_liner: 64-bit non-cryptographic hash built only from 32-bit operations. In pure JS it beats xxhash-wasm XXH64 on 4-8 byte keys.
what_it_does: A single public-domain C header (haya32x64.h) defines a seeded 64-bit hash. Its state, adds, xors and rotates are all uint32_t, and the only wide primitive is the full 64-bit result of a 32x32 multiply. The C API takes and returns [lo, hi] word pairs, with a uint64_t convenience wrapper and a one-shot-identical streaming state. The npm package (haya32x64 0.2.0, ESM, Node >=18) returns the digest as [low32, high32]. It ships a pure-JS engine built on Math.imul and 16-bit limbs, plus the C header compiled to a 1.8 KB wasm module that takes over from 16 bytes. It is a different function from xxHash or hayahash, so it is not a drop-in: switching changes every stored digest.
how_it_is_fast: Short keys (8 bytes or less) take a dedicated path of two complete 32x32 products, and the JS engine keeps inputs under 16 bytes out of wasm. That avoids the JS-to-wasm copy and call overhead that xxhash-wasm pays on every call, and it avoids BigInt. Inputs of 128 bytes or more use a 'pair-lane' kernel: four lane pairs over 32-byte blocks, where each 8-byte stripe feeds one complete 32x32 multiply, m = (u0 + a) * (u1 + b), with the product's low and high words cross-fed back into the lanes. Per the author's profiling, that halves instructions per byte compared with the earlier one-multiply-per-word kernel. The 16-127-byte mid path absorbs 16-byte stripes through four multiply lanes plus a serial carry, and a two-round Feistel seed premix keeps all 64 seed bits.
when_to_use: JavaScript hashing of very short binary keys (Uint8Array, 4-8 bytes) where you need 64 output bits without BigInt or wasm: 22.9 ns vs 39.4 ns for xxhash-wasm XXH64 at 4 B on EPYC 9R45
CSP-restricted or edge JS runtimes where WebAssembly may be unavailable: the pure-JS engine alone reaches about 3.9-4.5 GB/s at 1 MiB, over 100x the pure-JS xxhashjs XXH64 package (28-37 MB/s)
Cross-language digests that must match exactly between C, JS and wasm (bit-exact engines checked against 180 shared KAT vectors and a C-reference differential corpus)

32-bit targets without a 64-bit multiply (Cortex-M, RV32) or shaders, which are the stated design targets; in native SMHasher3 it is the fastest 32-bit-arithmetic row listed (7.50 B/cycle vs t1ha0 5.21 and XXH-32 4.89 on C8a)
Content fingerprints or cache keys in mixed JS/C systems where Unlicense/public-domain licensing matters
when_not_to_use: Any native 64-bit C/C++ host: XXH3-64 runs at 60.59 vs 7.50 B/cycle bulk, and rapidhash, wyhash and a5hash-128 are also faster on both small keys and bulk. The README itself says to use a 64-bit-native hash there

JavaScript string keys: through the string API xxhash-wasm is about 4.5x faster (59.2 ns vs 267.9 ns for 8 ASCII chars on C8a) because haya32x64 runs TextEncoder first; cyrb53 is 6.5 ns if 53 bits are enough

Bulk JS hashing where wasm is allowed: at 1 MiB on C8a, xxhash-wasm XXH64 (15,973 MB/s) and hayahash64 wasm (16,034 MB/s) beat the haya32x64 hybrid (10,971 MB/s). With 64 KiB chunks, xxhash-wasm streaming is about 3.7x faster than haya32x64's pure-JS-only stream

Persisted digests that must stay stable: the digest is labeled experimental and frozen only at an interim verification value (0x431563D2). Output for inputs of 128 bytes or more already changed between published releases (v0.1.x to v0.2.0)
Hash tables keyed by attacker-controlled data, or any authentication use: it is non-cryptographic and makes no keyed collision-resistance claim

integration.dependencies: none (C: stddef.h, stdint.h, string.h only; npm package has no runtime dependencies)
integration.min_toolchain: C11 as tested in CI (GCC, Clang, MSVC /std:c11; the header also compiles as C++11/C++17); Node.js >= 18 for the npm package
integration.platforms: any C target with uint64_t for the 32x32 product. CI covers x86-64, x86 ILP32, AArch64, big-endian s390x (qemu), MSVC x64 and wasm32. Endian-independent output. No Cortex-M, RV32 or GLSL builds are tested or shipped despite being the stated targets
integration.thread_safety: C: no global mutable state (all static inline functions over caller-owned haya32x64_state), so concurrent calls on distinct states are safe; not otherwise documented. JS: one module-level wasm instance per realm, which is safe because JS runs single-threaded per isolate

gotchas: Different digest from xxHash and from the same author's hayahash, so switching means migrating stored data. Digests of inputs 128 bytes and longer changed in v0.2.0 (pair-lane, then cross-feed kernel); digests under 128 bytes have been stable since the original 0xEAA8E435 version

The JS API returns [low32, high32] word pairs, not a BigInt or a 16-byte string; use haya32x64Hex/digestHex for hex. Strings passed to stream.update() are UTF-8 encoded one at a time, so a surrogate pair split across two calls hashes differently from the one-shot form

The hybrid engine copies every input of 16 bytes or more into one shared wasm memory that grows to the largest input seen and never shrinks (WebAssembly memory cannot shrink). Use haya32x64Pure or the ./pure export to avoid wasm entirely

The digest is defined only for lengths 0..UINT32_MAX. The C one-shot takes size_t but casts the length to 32 bits for the finalizer, and the streaming API requires the caller to keep the cumulative length within UINT32_MAX
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over xxHash (XXH64 via xxhash-wasm, or xxhashjs) and over its sibling hayahash only for JS code that hashes very short byte keys with no BigInt and optionally no wasm, or for hardware with only 32-bit multiplies. On 64-bit native hosts, and for JS bulk or string hashing where wasm is allowed, xxHash (XXH3/XXH64) or hayahash wins.
verified_claims_summary: On one AWS c8a.2xlarge (EPYC 9R45) and one c8g.2xlarge (Neoverse V2), Node.js 24.18 / V8 13.6, the author took medians of nine warmed public-API samples. The pure-JS engine hashed 4-byte Uint8Arrays in 22.9 / 34.0 ns vs 39.4 / 63.9 ns for xxhash-wasm 1.1.0 XXH64, about 1.7-1.9x (derived); at 8 B the gap is about 1.8-2.1x. XXH64 via wasm still led at 1 MiB (15,973 vs 10,971 MB/s hybrid on C8a) and on string inputs. Native SMHasher3 (GCC 15.2 -O3 -march=native) shows it far behind 64-bit-multiply hashes.
status_note: Active (last default-branch commit 2026-09-19, mostly dependabot), with 0 stars and about 28 npm downloads in the past month. It is a roughly 7-week-old solo-author project at v0.2.0 with an experimental digest, though the Unlicense single header is trivial to vendor and has an unusually thorough CI and test suite.
